baseline-survey: The survey counts as the first full sweep of the ledger audit; see “The ledger audit”. The brief records it just before the baseline is cut, the one moment when what the ledger holds and what the codebase does are known to agree. Pass --no-audit for a survey that is deliberately partial.
change-highlighting: There were two stripes, so a capability recorded late printed as new or updated. A capability that had been in the product for two years then read as this sprint's work, which is the one thing a client would take issue with. The grey stripe says what is actually true: the product did not move this cycle, the record did. Entries the ledger audit turns up are the usual case; see “The ledger audit”. It is a neutral grey rather than a fourth hue because green and blue are already spoken for, an accent in that band is refused for the same reason, and a fifth hue would leave a brand only reds, oranges, purples and browns to choose from.

Whether an entry printed as new or updated depended on whether it had change bullets. A new feature that picked up a change bullet during the release printed as updated, with a "What changed" note about a version the client never saw. It is now new whenever the feature first appears in that release, and a new entry never prints a change note.
init-a-ledger: Setup gitignored the client PDFs along with the Markdown docs, so the repo kept none of the editions handed over. A team that hands a printed edition to a client at each release wants the repo to hold what was handed over, so where the editions land is now a choice made once at setup.
pdf-edition: The contents list was a printed index: it named each area and how many features were in it, but reaching a section meant scrolling for it. Every line is now a link to the section it names, and the closing sections on what was withdrawn and what else changed are listed there too, because the edition is usually read on screen rather than on paper.

Every edition printed the ledger's own version number, starting from 1, so a project whose client already held reports sent another way before the ledger started handed them a second Version 1. A release can now set the number its edition prints, and later editions carry on from it; the ledger's own numbering is unchanged.

ledger build printed one PDF: the newest edition, or the open release as a draft once it had work in it, under the same file name and in the same folder the cut edition would use. A draft could be mistaken for the edition the client was handed. A draft is now named with -draft and kept out of the client folder, only ledger cut writes into it, and ledger build also prints any cut edition that isn't on disk.
product-wide-change: The command was ledger other-change. It is now ledger note, which names what it records; the old name still works and says what it is called now.
record-a-change: A change bullet could be added to a feature that was new in the same release, and a second change in one release got no warning. Each bullet then described the state just before its own update, which the client never saw, so an edition could explain a fix to something that was new in the same release. The command now refuses bullets on a new feature and reminds you which edition a second change is measured against.
release-editions: A release was a name and a date, and the date was doing work it could not do: two demos in one day are ordinary, and nothing said which of the two editions a reader was holding or which state of the code it came from. Every cut now records its commit. Sharing a date is still fine, but sharing a date and a commit is refused, because the two editions would stand for the same moment; --skip moment covers a deliberate re-issue.

A release could be cut as soon as it had something recorded against it, and nothing checked that its entries read correctly as one release. A cut now needs the release reviewed first, unless it is the first edition, and it also waits for the ledger audit and for any redraft to be checked. See “Reviewing a release before it goes out”, “The ledger audit” and “Redrafting the ledger”.

Cutting was ledger release cut followed by a separate ledger build, and a refused cut printed one line about the first problem it hit. That refusal was easy to miss: the build that followed printed the open release under the file name the cut edition would have had, so it looked as though the cut had worked. The command is now ledger cut, it prints the edition itself, and a refusal says plainly that the release was not cut and lists every open check at once.
status-check: ledger status showed what the open release held and warned about what would print badly, but it did not say whether the release could be cut: you found out by trying, one refusal at a time. It now shows the checklist ledger cut runs (see “Cutting a release”), and ledger on its own says where things stand and what to run next, so nobody has to remember the order of audit, review and cut.

compositions.overview: Version 3 changes how an edition is written and how it reads. Changes are recorded as facts while the work happens, and the text you read is written once per release, in one session that also finds unrecorded work and checks the text against the code. Each edition is now short: what moved in full, and one line for everything else.

init-a-ledger: Setup creates the same ledger as in v2, and its closing steps now have you read and commit the survey's entries and cut the first edition yourself; see “Baseline survey of an existing codebase”.
agent-wiring: The stanza now tells an agent to record what moved and why in a sentence a client could read, with how to see it when known, and never to commit, prepare or cut unless asked, because agents don't commit for you and the free preview reads well only if the recorded facts do.
baseline-survey: The survey used to cut the baseline itself and record the first audit; it now writes how to see each capability and stops before the cut without committing, because you read, commit and cut the baseline yourself, and there are no audits any more.
A survey that stops partway now carries on from the entries it already wrote instead of starting again, so the batches already written aren't paid for twice.
retone-brief: The rewrite brief covered every entry; it now covers only the entries still in the old tone and resumes from the areas left, because the tone of each entry is recorded rather than guessed, so no entry is rewritten into the tone it already has.
authoring-rules: The rules were the full guide to writing the ledger, notes for the client included; they now cover only what an agent recording a change needs, because those notes are written once per release and every line an agent reads is paid for on every edit.
record-a-capability: A new capability can now also record how to see it, the steps a reader follows to check the claim for themselves.
record-a-change: A change used to be recorded as a note written for the client as it landed; it is now two facts, what moved and why, and the edition's note is written once for the whole release, because a note written mid-release described a state the client often never saw; see “Preparing an edition”.
A change can now also say how to see the entry, so a client can check each claim for themselves.
editing-by-hand: Besides an entry's own words, you can now reword how to see it and an edition's notes, summary and message, because those are client-facing prose like the rest and are written for the whole release.
areas: An area can now open with a one-sentence overview in the edition's list of every feature, so the way the service is organized is clear.
agent-handoff: The agent tasks were bootstrap, audit, review, redraft check and style rewrite; the audit and the review are now steps of preparing an edition, and finding work nobody recorded is a task of its own; see “Preparing an edition” and “Finding work nobody recorded”.
product-wide-change: A product-wide note printed at the end of the edition; it is now listed on the first page and printed with the changes in detail, under Across the product, because a brief explanation of what changed is a good start to the document.
read-the-corpus: Showing an entry now also prints how to see it and its recorded changes, and can show it as it stood at any version or beside the last edition's text, which is what you need in front of you before saying what changed.
status-check: Status showed the checklist the cut ran; it now shows what the cut would refuse and what it would only warn about, and lists the reasons nobody has given, because the cut now warns instead of blocking.
Status now warns about a description that runs long for its size, because past two or three sentences an edition stops being brief.

Status also warns about client text that reads like code, such as a file name, and about a note, a summary item or an overview that runs long, because the people who read an edition are not necessarily technical.
release-editions: A cut refused to go ahead until five checks passed; it now refuses only an edition that would be wrong, with nothing recorded or a redraft not yet checked, and shows everything else before it asks, because what isn't done is your call and the tool's job is to say it clearly.
A cut now also writes the message to send beside the edition, and never hands work to a coding agent, so tokens are spent only when someone asks for them.
pdf-edition: An edition printed every entry in full; it now prints only what moved in full, with how to see it, and one line for every other feature, because reprinting unchanged entries made up most of an edition, 13 pages for 25 features in the second.
Each feature now carries one number that the first page, the details and the full list all cite, and the PDF has bookmarks, so you see at once what changed and find your way around without effort.
The first page now opens with a short overview of the release, and a new or changed entry can say why it matters to you, so the document is easier to read.
The list of every feature now opens on its own contents, each area with its count and how many of its features moved, so the document is easier to find your way around.
A draft now prints the recorded changes, marked as such, until the edition is prepared, because a draft with no notes hid the very changes it was printed to show.
markdown-docs: The Markdown documents now print how to see each entry under its description, because a description can leave you asking which part of the product it is about, and this answers that the same way every time.
change-highlighting: Each mark now prints as a word, New, Changed or Already in place, beside its colour, and the changes in detail are grouped in that order, so you see at once what changed.

matters.baseline-survey: Nothing is cut or committed until you have read it.
matters.record-a-capability: You can check each claim in the edition for yourself.
matters.record-a-change: A note can no longer describe a version of a feature you never had.
matters.areas: You can see how the service is organized before reading any entry.
matters.status-check: Nothing in an edition is written in terms only a developer would follow.
matters.pdf-edition: You get more of what you need from each page, and see what changed on the first one.
matters.markdown-docs: You can tell which part of the product an entry is about without asking.

new.text: Changes are recorded as facts, and written up once per release.
One command runs whichever agent task is due, or none at all.
Work nobody recorded is found by reading the code that changed.
Every entry can say how to check it for yourself.
A reason nobody gave stays a question until a person answers it.
The size of the open release shows without printing anything.
An older ledger upgrades in one step, and past editions print unchanged.

changed.text: Editions are short: what moved in full, everything else one line each.
Cutting a release warns instead of blocking, and writes the message.
The baseline survey stops for you to read, commit and cut it.
Status warns about long descriptions and text that reads like code.

compositions.message:
Version 3 of the feature-ledger feature ledger is attached.

What's new:
- Changes are recorded as facts, and written up once per release.
- One command runs whichever agent task is due, or none at all.
- Work nobody recorded is found by reading the code that changed.
- Every entry can say how to check it for yourself.
- A reason nobody gave stays a question until a person answers it.
- The size of the open release shows without printing anything.
- An older ledger upgrades in one step, and past editions print unchanged.

What changed:
- Editions are short: what moved in full, everything else one line each.
- Cutting a release warns instead of blocking, and writes the message.
- The baseline survey stops for you to read, commit and cut it.
- Status warns about long descriptions and text that reads like code.

No longer available: the ledger audit and the release review. Both are now steps of preparing an edition; the edition says more.
